population: Finnish men: Helsinki Birth Cohort Study (43 longer-living healthy, 92 who died of natural causes at mean age 66.6) plus 63 healthy men of mean age 83 from the Helsinki Businessmen Study
conclusion: The T allele was carried more often by the men who had died earlier than by the longer-living healthy men: 9 of 184 control alleles against 3 of 212 longer-living alleles, a combined prevalence odds ratio of 3.58 (95% CI 0.96-13.4, p = 0.074) in the direction of earlier death. Not significant at the study's own 0.05 threshold; the authors report 28.4% power and call for a larger cohort. Sequencing SIRT6 exons and their boundaries found this one SNP more abundant in the controls, and both of the paper's tables type it as an intron variant, 23 bases downstream of the exon 2 boundary.
statistical_test: two-tailed Fisher exact test on allele counts, HBCS and HBS combined (198 individuals: 106 longer-living healthy men vs 92 who died at mean age 66.6). ORIENTATION: OR 3.58 is the odds of the T allele in the EARLIER-DEATH control group relative to the longer-living group, so OR > 1 means T is associated with dying earlier, not with surviving. Reproduced from the published counts as (9/175)/(3/209) = 3.583, which confirms it is allelic and confirms the body's and Table 2's 3.58 over the abstract's 3.53.
provenance_quote: The T allele was present more often among subjects in the control group, i.e. those who died at an earlier age, than in the two groups of longer-living and healthy subjects combined.
effect_unit: prevalence odds ratio for the T allele in the earlier-death control group relative to the longer-living group

population: 227 community-dwelling adults aged 60-90 in Birjand, Iran, sampled from the Birjand Longitudinal Aging Study biobank (38 robust, 150 pre-frail, 39 frail)
conclusion: Across three age bands the T allele frequency was 1.39% at 60-69, 4.65% at 70-79 and absent at 80-90 (allelic Fisher p = 0.073); the 70-79 vs 80-90 comparison gave p = 0.06 and an odds ratio of 3.9. The same paper's primary question, frailty, showed no association (allelic Fisher p = 0.36, 8 of 376 non-frail alleles T against 0 of 78 frail). Exploratory; only 8 heterozygotes were seen and no T homozygote. Direction on the age axis agrees with the Finnish cohort, on the frailty axis it does not.
study_design: cross-sectional analysis within a case-control study embedded in the BLAS cohort
statistical_test: Fisher's exact test on allele frequencies across three age bands (60-69 / 70-79 / 80-90)
provenance_quote: The T allele was observed among individuals aged 60 to 80 years, but was absent in those older than 80.
